interactions.title: The Bahrazel call the debts and commission Hagrim’s judgment
lines: DM: A sort of emerging. The water almost begins to part a little bit. Emerging up out of out of the middle of the of the water, you see, like an anvil, a forge, the hammer pounding, the sound now echoing from the middle of the room, getting louder and louder. The smell of iron. You see a little silver tear drop spraying out in each direction every time the hammer hits the forge, shimmering and then landing, as they land in the water, sort of stretching out to make these long, delicate swords.

DM: The wind picks up, and you see the occasional spark of lightning in the sky above you, rather, the ceiling of the chamber. Ah! And as the as the forge sort of emerges fully formed, you can see that the water that's flowing off of that, in addition to these little silver tear drops that are spreading out, it seems to be you catch the smell of of cooking, of beer, of companionship, of dirt, soil, living things growing, and gradually you hear the you know the sound begin to shift from chanting your names to a voice. It's not, it's, it's— Ah, it's just a modulation of this sort of pounding from the rhythmic thumping of a hammer with the sort of names echoing to a voice, not a physical presence so much as just the sense that you are not alone.

DM: And floating sort of hovering in the in the air, drifting towards you. You each see this one of these silver raindrops kind of forms itself into almost um translucent sort of ephemeral. And this ethereal thing, and begins to drift towards Merash. Ah, a um! Some of the water begins. Water begins to flow from the chalice that Riswynn is holding into a hammer. But again a little translucent sort of an almost ethereal hammer sort of drifts over towards Riswynn.
DM: Iron bands. Um! Like a tankard, but with an iron band like a ring wrapped around the middle of it, drifts over towards Rothfis,
DM: And ah! Let's see. I forget the the details of I don't know if you added any details to what I said, but something that would represent your characters' debt of— debt to the gods.
Thror: Yeah, maybe it's like a broken ship.
DM: Okay, I'm— like a small sort of broken ship drifting uh drifting towards Thror.
DM: Um, it has these, uh— as these little um spiritual tokens begin to drift towards you. This voice speaks: Your debts are called. You have answered. Watch.
DM: Listen. And everything goes still for a moment.
DM: It's clearly the presence of
DM: The Bahrazel here speaking to you,

DM: And the water clears, and you see an image. This chalice that Riswynn is holding, ah, floating in the— it's floating in the— [garbled] Here, this chalice. Link in chat, from floating, and then images flashing forward, telling its story,

DM: Marking the marking the place of safety in this new kingdom formed by refugees from war. Um group of dwarven soldiers setting out with this chalice going north, a vision of of people gathering of names and lists of those who are lost, those refugees who were not found who never made it to safety, and dwarves, setting out north with this chalice to find and bring them back. Um, the march home. Hundreds of dwarfs sustained by the chalice, a fire giant bearing down upon them, screaming about vengeance for his father, trolls with him, descending, the dwarves fleeing to a massive statue, maybe fifty feet tall, of a stoneborn and building hasty fortifications around the base of the statue, a grim warrior bearing a large two-handed axe and an iron helm leading the way, and then flames flickering, the end of the fight.

DM: Fire giant, victorious, laughing as dwarf fights dwarf, the grim warrior with the axe standing on a pile of the dead, attacking all who come to him. Dwarves, trolls alike, screaming, "Death in battle is all that is left!" The fire giant falling and another dwarf turning to confront this warrior, the flames consuming them as they fight, the smoke gradually growing thicker and thicker as grim warrior, the hundreds of refugees, the trolls, everything left flickers out one by one, until all you can see is smoke.
DM: And then the voice speaks again:
DM: Hagrim was lost that day,
DM: His evil deeds taking him to a place we cannot reach, a domain, uh, part of the Shadowfell.

DM: Your quest, then: to go there, find him. Hagrim his name. Now that the chalice has been restored and found again, confront him. Either send him to damnation or forgiveness with the waters of life.

DM: You are emissaries. It is up to you to decide his fate. Taking this quest, your debt to us is fulfilled. It is upon your honor to decide how you proceed. You're not compelled to die in our service. Succeed or fail, you may redeem your bond, and it will return you to your home.
DM: These four spirit representations of the of your debts drift and sort of merge with you, and you know that, as this happens, you know that you have a choice,
DM: And if you decide to leave, this will take you back,
DM: The gods judge, and those who dishonor themselves will the— face other other trials in the future.

DM: Ah! And then, um, the images fade and the water turns to mist, and you can see through the mists, um, a muddy river, cliff, jagged cliffs, a shadowy realm, and the gods, the voice of the gods fades and leaves you to your companions.

Rothfis: Ah! During everything that just transpired, Rothfis would have uncorked the keg and poured himself a drink and had it, and poured himself another drink and had it. He looked around and he said it. So it— so succeed or fail, we get to go home. I— are any of you here not, not by our own will? I— I thought, I didn't ever think I'd have to pay a debt to my ex-wife's family. I just want to go home to my tavern, and—

Merash: I think that, uh, Rothfis is kind of outburst there. Merash had her hand out, and was just about to touch the wispy, ephemeral drop that had been going towards her. It glinted on the blade of her knife, and before she could do anything she sort of snapped out of it, and just sort of looks around at this and goes, "This is something I never thought would come to pass, and I don't want to be here. I don't want to fulfill my debt," but the mists just sort of have fallen into this muddy river, jagged cliff mirage, and she just is lost and looks defeated.
Rothfis: Well, two are the same, I guess. Would you like a pint?
Merash: Merash puts out her hand, and has a small cup that she passes over to Rothfis.
Rothfis: Rothfis Stonefist. Nice to meet you. Not Ironcorn, not Ironcorn.
Merash: Amberfoot. It is, I must say, not a pleasure.

Thror: Thror laughs bitterly, and then sits down right where he is, shaking his head. I swear myself to the Bahrazel, Bahrazel, the to atone for the terrible things I'd done, for a life misspent, for pain inflicted. It's just that that was yesterday, and I didn't think this was going to come quite so quick. I'm glad to be here. If it means I can go home again.

Riswynn: There is never a good time for a call from the gods. I fear for what is going on with my companions back where I came from. But life of service to my clan and my gods, and here I am at this moment, which is not my choice. But there seems to be a path that way. Starting a journey can see it finished sooner. Back to what our plans are.
Rothfis: Rothfis pours another two cups and pushes them in your two directions. I think if we're going to be a party, for however short or long, we should all join together and cheers to our fates.
Riswynn: It's, it's, it's stone, but it's— Thank you.

before: Merash: Uh, so when you look over towards Merash, just a little bit away from Rothfis, you see someone, um, with patchy skin, looking almost like there's a a pattern of spotting and scar tissue working up their arms up into their face, and they are so just halfway through, stropping their small knife with a leather strop as if they had been in the middle of their work day. Um! And as they sort of get their feet around them and realize where they are, you just see a look of resignation, almost of a an expectation that this was coming.

Riswynn: That Thror? Okay. So, ah, there's a a heavily armored dwarf, you know, ready for adventure. Red hair bound up, you know, able to be out of the way in a fight, and she looks like she's been in the situation of distress and and strain, and she's holding in her hand a chalice of— looking at this chalice like, "What have you done?" Because what was expected did not result, and again, like Merash, she looks unsurprised that there are hammers pounding in the background, still caught up in the moment that she was in before being found in this cave instead.

Thror: Thror is deeply tanned and smelling of salt and sea, with the hair and beard braided back and away from his face. He's got a dipper of water to his mouth that he was clearly in mid-drink, and he's just frozen um barefoot sailor-style, but strange for a dwarf in the middle of a giant cavern.

DM: As you look around at each other, the water begins to ripple slightly, um, and then, and over the course of this, as you're sort of all on like four sides of the this big pool in the middle, just kind of looking, looking across at each other. Um,
Unknown: To the
after: DM: Anybody walking through the mists? Okay,

Riswynn: Get a rope out of my pack and say, "I don't know what lies ahead, and I don't know what's been provided on each of our backs. But if we're going to do this together, maybe we should hang on to something." Does it seem like there's not a mist, we can't see where we're going? Or is it just like a passage? You know, you can't see where you're going. I—

DM: I mean, there, you can see like occasionally through— every now and then it'll clear a little bit, and there's like a muddy, a muddy river bank. That seems like what you would appear next to if you stepped through the veil, but it's dim and shadowy.
Merash: I resignedly, looped my hand through the length of rope,
Thror: And with shake of his head and a rueful smile Thror grabs it, too.

interactions.title: Rothfis recalls the lost rescue expedition and chalice
lines: DM: Oh, there we go. Okay, um, yeah. I mean, you've heard, you've heard tales of the Shadowfell. You've certainly heard, you've heard tales of this— Ah, of this whole series of events, right? So there was. This was maybe one hundred and fifty years ago. Um. Maybe two hundred years ago there was this massive war. One of the dwarven kingdoms got basically completely destroyed, overrun by aberrations from the deep. The dwarfs all fled south.

DM: And some thirty, forty years after they fled south, there was a famous expedition led by, um— Ah, this a young dwarf, like sort of hotshot commander Nora Sparksilber, and a veteran of the wars, a veteran of the great war, who had come back, after fighting mind flayers and other crazy things deep underground, had sort of been a bit of a hero who traveled with Nora. This was Hagrim— traveled with Nora north.

DM: There were many, many dwarves who never made it south, so there was a mission to hopefully um find those who could be found. Um! This Chalice of the Runepriest was brought, as its water sustains you, has healing properties, or so it was thought. But the warband never returned, none of the refugees ever returned, and the chalice was lost, for hundreds of years, and that after that event the refugee dwarfs, the dwarves who had established the new kingdom, sort of turned their back on the ruins, wrote it off as too dangerous, not willing to risk any others.
Rothfis: Uh you, said Hagrim, Silver Spark? Is there two different people? Nora Sparksilber, who was the young hotshot commander of the war bands that went north.

DM: She was the leader, but Hagrim Firebrand was the sort of hero of the previous war. An old veteran who went as kind of the champion and and, um, called out of retirement somewhat reluctantly. Sort of travel, traveled north. Ah! A sort of heroic face of the expedition under the command of Nora Sparksilber. Uh, and you actually, since you're um Rothfis, since your inn is in Chardon, and you'd actually heard rumors you thought unsubstantiated about the recovery of this chalice. About a year ago there was supposedly some wizard at the University, who was like telling tall tales that you attributed to just tall tales, since it had been lost for hundreds of years, but apparently—well, Riswynn is now holding the chalice so clearly not entirely tall tales.

before: DM: But yes, it is reminiscent of that for sure.
DM: So where do you want to go? And as you started to, just like to be clear, all your adventuring equipment comes with you, if you, even if you didn't have a—

Rothfis: Could Rothfis do a History or something to, um, to think of stories of this he's heard in the tavern, or would know the Shadowfell, or of this specific battle and everything we've been told about.
DM: Sure.
Rothfis: Okay, let me see if I'm still linked up through the Beyond20, all right. That was quick, sweet. It's up to your Internet.
after: Rothfis: Very cool.
Unknown: So

DM: You're all standing on the banks of this river, starting to sink slowly into the mud. There are lights ahead of you, campfires and lanterns. There's an ashy plain to your right and cliffs to your left and a giant statue in the distance.
Riswynn: Despite an uncertain welcome from those lanterns and campfires, it's probably safer than poking through this pile of bones, looking for information.
Thror: Let's say hello. I agree.

interactions.title: The guard explains patrols and announces the strangers
lines: DM: You get maybe a hundred feet. You, you get about halfway across the sort of open stretch from behind this, this little outcropping to towards the village, when when one of them, one of these four dwarves, stops, sort of turns slowly to look at you and like blinks um kind of shakes his head and looks up at you, says, "Who are you?"
Riswynn: And we, in a decently loud voice, "Peace of the Bahrazel to you. We're finding ourselves newly in these parts. Can you tell us about your home?"
DM: Sort of blinks a few times and steps forward again, and he says, "You are— You are not from Morkalan."

DM: Looks over, and one of the other guards kind of shakes her head, and one of the two carrying a badly made sword, and she looks, looks over at him, and she like slowly nods. And then she just begins to walk into the river. But towards and across the river, basically, there seems to be a ford or a shallow spot here.
DM: "What brings strangers to these parts? Do not see—" It seems to be like thinking for a moment, like trying to remember a word. "Outsiders very often."
Merash: We are looking for our friend. Maybe you know him.
DM: You have a friend? I do not know. What is friend?
DM: A few on the cliffs. We don't speak. The woman who left is now like halfway across the river.
Riswynn: Does your party guard against outsiders or some other danger in these parts, or the people on the cliff?
DM: Soldiers guard. We are soldiers, I think.
Rothfis: And where is she going? Point to the one moving across the river. What's she guarding?
Rothfis: Do any of us know that name?
DM: It's just what the Bahrazel told you the name of this Shadowfell domain is.
Rothfis: This is my entire domain. A better—[garbled] at best.
Riswynn: At this point—go ahead—saying to you, you all of them aside, "Perhaps we don't want to make the acquaintance of Morkalan."
Merash: Are the people on the cliff outsiders too?
Thror: Do you know who's on the cliff?
DM: I don't—others spoke. Morkalan, Morkalan told us once to tell them things, and we did, but not me. Others.
DM: Why are— Why are you here? I must continue my patrol. It is important, I think, Morkalan will be angry if the forms are not kept.
Riswynn: You don't need to disturb your patrol duties any longer. We had hopes there might be a settlement here where we could meet folk and and converse. But you seem busy.
Rothfis: Is there a safe way up the cliffs? The—
DM: I was not sent on that patrol. Others do that duty.
Riswynn: Where are the messengers who do that duty?
Riswynn: Please hold that to many.
DM: I I must patrol. I will not stop you. You will be announced, and that is all that Morkalan cares. You may pass or leave as you choose, but I will go.
DM: He turns, he starts walking again.
Thror: I'll say that to the patrolling Dwarf before we go on. Where's your commanding officer?

DM: Blinks, and for a minute, you see, like a like a look of what seems like real sadness on his face. Just a ghost now, I think. And he sort of pauses for a moment. I have not seen him in a long time. They're all ghosts now.

DM: Kind of shakes his head for a moment. What did you say? Um, did you— Ah, it's like— turns back away from my— I— I must continue now. I, I, I, Morkalan will be angry, continues walking away from you.

before: Thror: Yeah, "Same," says Thror, holding up his totally empty hands.
Riswynn: Well, then, we'll go first.
DM: You walk forward, and and as you begin to approach, I mean you are the two plate-armored, heavy-weapon-carrying dwarves are not quiet.
Merash: We're clanky.
Thror: And—
after: Rothfis: I don't like this. I just want to say it before we move on. I don't want to get announced to it. Giant statue, or whatever it is,

Riswynn: The path up the cliffs will probably be faster, safer than scrambling up right now on ropes to be attacked while we're dangling on handholds and footholds by a giant statue. I say we see the path.

DM: So you pass the guards then, and enter into the sort of central chamber of the village, and this is arrayed, as many relatively small dwarven villages are, with sort of an entry chamber, and then it opens into a larger cavern. Um, that has both, ah, some buildings sort of in the on the cave floor kind of stacked three, four stories high, climbing up the sides, and then as well some some dwellings and other buildings that have been carved directly out of the cliff. So, as you enter, as you end, pass through this sort of entryway cliff and open into this, um, larger expanse. It's maybe a, you know, a large cavern, maybe a few hundred feet across, and maybe thirty feet tall.

DM: Um, you can see. So you see a few things. First of all, there are signs of life here, right? You can hear. Ah, you know the occasional rustle of movement, low whispered voices you can hear coming from what seemed to be one of the better, one of the better maintained houses, sort of off from the main village square a little bit. What sounds like a low, quiet, sobbing somebody um trying to like somebody crying into a pillow. Basically that kind of like muffled sobbing. Um, you know, the occasional sound of a door closing, opening, everything muffled, but definitely more, you know. Every now and then you'll, you know, you're just kind of standing here kind of taking in. You see one, you—an older dwarven woman, kind of limping slowly across kind of looks at you startled, and then quickly darts into the building that she was going to um. You also see

DM: At the back of this cavern there's a another tunnel that goes forward and looks like it begins to slope off slightly. It's probably, uh, you know, this could— this could house several hundred dwarfs, four, five, six hundred, something like that, in your estimation, but lots of it is in very poor repair. Only a handful of houses seem to be actively maintained. There's no shops, there's no taverns. There's no— and there's a well in the center of the village square, which is fairly typical, but otherwise there doesn't seem to be any obvious signs of commerce or or industry.

interactions.title: The old woman refuses Rothfis’s ale
lines: DM: You knock on the door, and like pulls it open like a tiny bit, so she can. She can peer out, and she's probably at least two hundred, maybe older. Her hair has gone totally white, is like tied up in a long ponytail in the back, wrinkled gray face. Uh, leaning over, you know a little bit, looks at you and says, "No strangers," goes to shut the door.
Rothfis: And I guess I reach out more quickly than you would expect, and I put a hand on the door, and I say, How can we be strangers if we bring ale?
DM: There's no ale in this place. Tricksters.
Rothfis: I start pouring out of my mug just like a few drips in front of her. I say, "Not a trick, a treat."
DM: She kind of goes to shut the door again, and she says, "Mead, maybe. Don't care for ale." Slams the door shut.

before: DM: Um! But then, you know, sort of in the center and and sort of opposite side of the village from the one little well-maintained area there's like a mix of buildings that are not falling apart, but not—I mean nothing here is pretty, but um her house is one of the um not falling apart, but not like particularly nice. The sobbing seems to be coming from one of the nicer the like nice, well-mai—not nice, but like the well-maintained section, and most of the sort of much a lot of the muffled noises are coming from that section as well like the occasional door closing, or like something being set on a table or cough, low voices.

Riswynn: I'd rather not spend time talking to someone given in so much to this environment that they for a little— are like the guard and sort of lost in in in their place. So if the old woman's house is well enough maintained that she looks like she could hold a coherent conversation, whether those things actually correlate, then I think it's worth trying, or we can just go knock on the nicest door we see either way. We have a lovely flask to offer.
Merash: Well, at least we know that she would be behind that door as well. The other ones are a bit more of a crapshoot.
DM: That's a good choice, folks.
Riswynn: Knock on the door and ask if you like a drink.
after: Rothfis: Well, that went well.
Unknown: It could have been worse.
Rothfis: Right, and not stabbed.
Riswynn: You're not stabbed. That's the spirit. Let's look for a thirstier neighbor.
DM: Pick a random house.

interactions.title: Dworic trades news of Bleakhold and Tak for ale and cheese
lines: DM: You knock on the door, here, I— muttering under breath in Dwarvish, like it sounds like a the elderly voice of an elderly man. "Who could that be?" Now it— One moment.
((Interjections and repeated names or supply bookkeeping))

DM: ((Smith and sword description)) and he looks surprised, shocked almost to see your shining armor and your weapons, and your, Riswynn's shield. And just you're like the sort of quality of your gear says, "Who are you?"
Merash: We are newcomers to town, and we heard the sounds that possibly you might have a bit of a shop that we might be able to speak with you over, perhaps a strop to lend?
DM: Wouldn't call it a shop, but come in. Come in. Don't just stand there, somebody will see you.
Merash: What are we not doing here?
DM: Well, I guess you probably can't leave at this point, so it's only a matter of time,
Merash: All right, I'd kind of go inside in. What could go wrong?
DM: He sort of like bows slightly to the two women, and he says, "Dworic at your service, such as it is."
DM: Just shakes his head. Merash
DM: And these—poorly equipped fellows trailing behind you.
Rothfis: Poorly equipped? And I offer him a pint. It's your plate.
((Interjections and repeated names or supply bookkeeping))
Rothfis: I never joke about ale,
Rothfis: There's more where that came from.
DM: Sits down like, puts his feet up, takes a sip, just sighs for a moment.
DM: That takes me back. It seems that ale is hard to come by here. Can't remember to when, but it's familiar somehow.
((Interjections and repeated names or supply bookkeeping))
DM: He looks puzzled for a moment.
((Interjections and repeated names or supply bookkeeping))
DM: Beyond the village? What— Where did you come from? I haven't seen new dwarves in many a year. Is there another city somewhere in this world?
Merash: It's a bit complicated where we're from, but we're hoping that we're able to pass through. You seem to not want us to be seen. Is there something that we should know of?
Merash: And Morkalan is a dwarf? A being?

DM: I feel like I knew once. Now he, a sometimes just speaks. Anyone here could become Morkalan in a moment speaking commands test our loyalty. Those who disobey, into the ash fields for the trolls. So if he has not met you yet, there will be a test coming, I am sure. Can't imagine it would be a pleasant test. Stay outside.
Riswynn: What do you know of the dwarfs on the hill? We heard some messengers from this village had been sent.

DM: Dwarves? No, humans up there, wanderers, we're calling to— rightly, saying, I— I feel like I once knew of a place that was not Bleakhold. Okay, they wander in sometimes, paying little mind, but they always seem lost. We call it the lost camps up there. Every now and then Morkalan will possess somebody and go up, and you tell them he has the secret of what they're looking for. I don't know what they're looking for in the lost camps. To be found again, maybe. And they'll look for a minute hopeful, and then Morkalan will leave, and there's just a confused dwarf standing there. No recollection of how they got to the camps unaware of anything to help those poor souls.
Merash: So there's no one in town who actually knows how to get there?
DM: Oh, there, there's a road. Like, just go out the back of the village and go up. It's very easy. Sort of laughs. That at least I can tell you, in exchange for the ale.
Merash: We appreciate that. How often does Morkalan send a dwarf up?
DM: Not often, since the mad priest left, it's less and less. I can't really say when that was, though
Riswynn: Did the mad priest go to the ashes,
((Interjections and repeated names or supply bookkeeping))
DM: I think he knew some secret, and it drove him mad. He refused to show his loyalty, and he wasn't killed. Well, I guess he's probably dead in the ash fields now.

Rothfis: I say, um, "Thanks for what you've provided so far. But, uh, perhaps we could trade a little more info for a little more ale. We're looking for some a clan named Firebrand or Sparksilber. Have you heard of those names?"
Rothfis: Or how about Hagrim or Nora?

DM: I don't know of them. Hagrim? Nora? To now are there— You think there are dwarfs who don't live in Bleakhold? I've wondered that. Rurik's boy, Tak. He thinks there's other dwarves out there, too. He thinks there's more than just us. Maybe he'd know. The mad priest raved about the—I remember this now. Why do I remember that place? What did he call it? Yuvanti? Maybe, he said, that was his real home. But there's no such place.
((Interjections and repeated names or supply bookkeeping))
Riswynn: Rurik's boy, he lives next door.
DM: Can I have that ale now, please? Some more.
DM: Or bread or cheese if you've got it.
((Interjections and repeated names or supply bookkeeping))
Rothfis: A— Take it slow with this one. It's an aged blue that you'll probably kick your shoes right off your feet. It's more mold than cheese. It's just like a big—
DM: And he's sizing for the first time. It looks like he just kind of opens his eyes, and his face lights up, and then—tasted anything like that in my life before. I thank you.
Rothfis: You're welcome, and if you're ever in Chardon don't don't be, don't be a stranger at Stonefist, Steins and Stables. It's always a pint there for you.
DM: There is no—okay. He looks just confused about that string of words, kind of sighs takes out his blade and starts sharpening it again. Just kind of out of a habit more than anything else.
((Interjections and repeated names or supply bookkeeping))
Rothfis: Go ahead. I was gonna say, um, do you think Tak will see us or should— Could you invite him over here to join us?
DM: I don't know, he's, uh, that boy likes to wander. I haven't seen him for day or two?
Merash: Where does he normally wander to?

DM: Up the river, says that's a keeps looking for other dwarfs, and for ghost of his mother, he says. The ghosts never leave here. I guess we'll all be ghosts one day. Land of ghosts at least. I've had some ale and cheese before my time. Thank you for that.
Rothfis: The least we could do for you. Setting us straight.
((Interjections and repeated names or supply bookkeeping))
DM: I don't know that I have more to tell you. Goes back to sharpening this blade

before: Unknown: Um.

DM: There's no doesn't seem to be any fire, or you don't hear bellows or anything like that. So it's probably just like straightening a blade, just, you know, gently with, um, cold, cold honing. But you definitely, that's the—there's the sobbing sound, and there's the somebody repairing some piece of metal sound are the two nicest houses.
Thror: I'm more intrigued by repairing of a blade. I feel like there might be common ground there.
Riswynn: Let's go talk shop, and do for a—
Merash: [garbled]
after: Rothfis: Definitely. It's not like a plus six weapon or something, right? It's not like a what? Like a super magic weapon. No, no,
DM: It looks like a sword that's been sharpened to within an inch of its life
Rothfis: Over. You know, it's gone from like this big to like that thing. He's turned the box into a rapier.
Unknown: I was—
Merash: I mean I'm tempted to go try to speak with Tak [garbled]—

interactions.title: Rurik entrusts the search for his son to the newcomers
lines: DM: Um, this is at least at least three rooms, and it goes. It's up against the wall of the cave, and then goes back, and, unlike, ah, the smith's house, where he seemed perfectly content to just rely on dark vision and see everything in shades of gray. Um! There's a lantern here, and you can see that there's like a few splashes of color, even like there's a a red blanket that's worn to bits, and as you, you, as the door sort of swings open, a dwarf of indeterminate age, maybe at least middle-aged, who's been kind of was dressed in just plain, plain sort of clothes. Nothing fancy, drab. Wears a silver ring around his neck. Again, I haven't seen anybody else with jewelry or adornments, or anything, and he he looks up from the table in the middle of the room that you enter as the door swings open. He yes,
DM: Kind of dries his eyes a little bit. Who are you? Why do you bother me? No one is ever here to help, so please be gone.
Merash: We just spoke with your neighbor, and he mentioned that you and your boy might know of dwarves not from here.
DM: He like sort of grit, grits his teeth a little bit. This meddling busybody. If he hadn't encouraged him, he would still be here.
Merash: Do you speak of your boy?
DM: Why, it damn smith, putting stories in his head,
DM: ((Interface troubleshooting)) He kind of stops, scoffs at you and says, If you're not here to help, just go leave me tonight. Leave me.
Riswynn: Perhaps were we to break bread and talk a bit, you could tell us about your boy, and we could help find him. We're good at looking for folks.
Thror: It's over. You could get all those ideas out of his head once and for all.

DM: Where are you from? No one in Bleakhold has ever offered to help anyone before. He looks puzzled, and then he, like sort of opens his eyes again, and seems to be taking in your appearance. He says again, "Where are you from?"
Merash: We are new to Bleakhold, and just looking for a friend.
DM: Well, wait, did you say break bread?
Rothfis: I've got some ale and a bit of cheese. Rothfis Stonefist at your service.
DM: Rurik. It's work. Kind of shakes his head again. He looks over at all of you. I know this is one of Morkalan's tricks, but can't give up hope yet. How would you find him?
Riswynn: Start by telling us what he looks like.

DM: He sighs. I guess he's not so young anymore. Almost your age, and he looks at, um, Merash. He's a— he's a lithe fellow, fast gray skin, gray hair, but striking blue eyes, a warm face. Not that it's something you see here much. Keeps his hair short. Hardly a beard at all.
Rothfis: So that's how he looks. Where do you think he might have gone?
DM: Sort of shakes his head, and kind of comes out of his reverie. How do I know you're not just Morkalan? Well, go find him yourself. Take him!
Merash: We haven't yet been met or seen by Morkalan.
Thror: But if we were, we really need you to help us find him.
DM: He only can see through our eyes. Can't read minds. So, yes, you would need me to speak his location.
Rothfis: I say, does Morkalan even know a good dwarven ale, do you think? Look at us. Look how colorful we are! Look how full of life and vibrance! I don't think we're Morkalan. Deal.
DM: I don't know what to think.
DM: Um! He looks. He looks around. Let me taste that ale.
Rothfis: Yeah, of course. Where is the biggest cup in your house? I just like to get to work. Ready?
DM: He looks around, and there's like this small sort of clay mug he puts down.
Rothfis: We'll have to do two or three of those then. Pour the brackish water out of it.
DM: He like takes a sip. And cheese, you said?
Rothfis: I, and I offer him a similar whatever I've got, like the old apron.
DM: Takes a bite and he sort of sighs. You're right. I do not think Morkalan can summon such things. You are all too too fresh and young. How did you get so young?
DM: Okay, so directed at the three, not four. Well, usually goes north. He likes to wander. He— he talks to ghosts, so many ghosts. The dead never leave, you see. They can't, I don't think.
Merash: Could we see the ghosts if we're not from here?
DM: I I am sure you could. There, ghosts like anything else. You'll be from here soon enough, I guess. The ghosts I don't think they like to be reminded of what passes for living here.
Merash: How long ago did your boy last leave from here?

DM: Almost four days? He's never been gone more than two before, said he had found somebody to the North talking about other worlds stories from a battle. I haven't fought any battles. Sounded like the mad priest.
DM: I— I yelled at him. I told him it was nonsense, stories his imagination. Dworic encouraged it. He liked the stories. He knew they weren't real. Tak said they weren't, ran.
DM: I'm afraid he— I don't know where he went. Up the river. Talk to them ghosts who told him stories, I guess. I hope anyway. Hope he didn't go looking for the mad priest in the ash fields.
Riswynn: No one knows if the mad priest is dead, but everyone thinks it's most likely.
DM: If he were dead, I think we would have seen his ghost.

Rothfis: It sounds like your boy may have met some of the folks we're looking for. Would you like to write him a letter or give us something of his that would let him know that you're thinking of him? If we do find him.

DM: I mean pauses for a minute, and he goes into the other room. Um the bedroom, and he he um comes back with this little something wrapped in a little piece of cloth, and he unfolds, and it is a poorly made, um, sort of crudely sculpted of, of clay, a pair of soldiers, like toy soldiers, um, but painted somehow with like red, reds and, and brown pigments. He used to imagine such battles, play. I always wished I could have made him more. But somehow even this took more effort. But he will recognize these anywhere.
DM: He looks around. Have no paper.
Rothfis: Sure, one of us would if you wanted to. Yeah, jot a quick note down,
DM: He writes just a quick like five, six lines, and and then ties it up, and then folds it and hands it to you and says, "Thank you."
Rothfis: Thank you for trusting us with this. We'll do what we can.
DM: Maybe there is. Maybe there is something you can do. I'll believe it when I see it. But thank you for giving an old man hope.

DM: Kind of closes his eyes as he, as he sits there, and you think, it occurs to you, there's something you slightly strange going on here, in that— So the the way he was describing Tak you'd guess he was probably, you know, so forty, something like that. He is almost um Merash's age, which is like fifty. Most of you, most of the younger ones of you are like between fifty and seventy, and but of course, Tak is, in the dwarven culture, these like single-syllable diminutive names are child's names, and by the time they're in their twenties they should have gone through the rite of name-taking and and gone to the the heart of the mountain, and here is like a forty-year-old who still seems to be a child. Strikes you as you get the note from him, and the soldier toys.
Riswynn: Time moves strangely here. Anyway, if anyone can be forty or fifty, if these people have been lost, well, I guess if newcomers can come in and get absorbed, okay, might ever hold we still—
Thror: Are we still there talking to him? Like, is that, was that— awesome. Yeah, you you said he left four days ago. Have you kept a record of how many days you've been here?
DM: He like looks confused at. I think I was born here, but I don't know when that was. There's no calendars.
DM: Tak was born forty years ago. His mother died ten years ago. I don't remember much before he was born.
DM: I can't remember my parents. I must have had parents. Maybe they died when I was young. I don't know
Thror: Your wife is a ghost now, then?
DM: Tak keeps looking for her. I know better than to bother the dead, but he is a boy I don't know if he has found her.
Merash: Well, I think if that is all the information that you have, we can be on our way to try to find your boy.

before: Riswynn: If it's the house next door, as long as he tells what's left or right, then maybe we can sneak that way without being seen too much
Thror: Big.
DM: Yeah, it's, it's left. It's the house that the sobbing is coming from.
Riswynn: All right. Let's head to the sobbing house before Riswynn can't resist the urge to reforge that sword any longer.

DM: So you knock on the door next door. So as you knock on it the door just kind of swings open like it hasn't, it's not locked or barred, or anything, and as you knock it, just creaks open, and you can see this is a larger house than the one next door that I'm— the smith's house was basically just a single room with a bed. Um, just his like, you know, tools.
after: Thror: Go ahead. And
DM: So the way he described it, um, uh, Tak had tended to travel
Unknown: Like

DM: Beyond the like north. Not the way you came from, I mean. There's not really a clear sense of direction here, but beyond where you— ah! beyond where you had been, not the direction you came from, but beyond the village, in the same direction you were walking when you got here. There's not much to see. There's no hardly any landmarks besides the river, and of course the massive statue with the piles of bones at its base, which is a few miles north of here.
Riswynn: If the guards were near the river on one side of town, but it's possible to leave in the on the other side of town, maybe, where there aren't guards, which is something to hope for.

interactions.title: Could the chalice take villagers to safety?
lines: Riswynn: So I'm beginning to wonder what would happen if they drank out of the chalice.
Rothfis: I had an interesting idea, but how would we? But they would get teleported to, they would get teleported to safety,
Thror: Leaving everyone else behind. Hmm.
Riswynn: But that doesn't even involve drinking, just touching.

before: Rothfis: But another ale.
DM: I like this character.
Rothfis: No, thanks. I'm enjoying them, too.
DM: Tak having some food and drink is turning out to be more useful than I expected.
Rothfis: Yeah, thanks for that,
after: Thror: Been trying to visualize the—where is the keg like on your person? Is it like you—
Rothfis: Oh, it's like, uh, yeah, yeah, like. Imagine you know, like when, when hear these with the, with the drums. It's sort of, it's wrapped like, like one of those like djembes would be.
Thror: I like, like a sort of like a this size kind of thing.
Rothfis: Yeah, exactly like a like a wooden keg about, you know, two or three feet tall and a foot wide. I was probably going to refill it right before I got pulled away.

DM: Okay, so we pick up as you leave the village to the north. Um. Heading, I assume, relatively, quietly, as best you can, not drawing attention to yourself, anyway, north along the river. And as you walk,

interactions.title: Tak reads his father’s letter and leads the way to Nora
lines: DM: So silence falls. You hear like a little plunk like a small rock being pushed out from the rockslide, and a shaky voice, "Hello?"
Thror: Hey, you okay in there?
((Brief interjections and postcombat healing or resource bookkeeping))
Thror: I think we have a note from your dad
DM: A couple more plunks as two more rocks get pushed out, and, like you see, an eye appear on the like like right here, like right in the mouth of this rock cave. Come closer. Let me see.
((Brief interjections and postcombat healing or resource bookkeeping))
DM: Eye disappears for a second.
((Brief interjections and postcombat healing or resource bookkeeping))
DM: Sounds of somebody thinking. Are the old ones gone?
((Brief interjections and postcombat healing or resource bookkeeping))
DM: Pauses for a moment. Couple rocks. You hear a couple of rocks shift. Hand sticks out. Let me see it. The letter.
Rothfis: Are we going to put this letter in the first hand that, that goes out of a rock? Or do we need a little more confirmation?
Thror: How about we do it this way? What's your father's name?
DM: Tak. Let me see it.
DM: And disappears. Two minutes, like a brief like gasp, sob. Eye comes back like looking around. I'm coming out. It's safe?
Thror: I mean, nothing is immediately trying to kill you. I don't know if it's safe more generally.

DM: Minutes ago. Rocks shift, like five minutes later, like this youngish-looking dwarf, short gray hair, all tightly tightly curled, tightly tied up, wearing sort of dusty clothes, striking blue eyes moving like— but his body language and actions seem younger than his than his physical appearance, looks up at you as he crawls out, "Dwarves! My father sent you."
Merash: We told your father that we would try to find you.
DM: Where are you from? Not here? Are the stories true? There are other dwarves? You must not be from Bleakhold.
DM: Where are you from? Tell me.
Merash: That is maybe a story for another pint of ale.
Rothfis: Oh, sonny, have you ever had water?
Rothfis: Well, this is a real treat that— I pour him a flagon.
DM: But he takes a sip. Yes, you drink that?
Rothfis: The youth is wasted on the young, and I pull it back.
DM: You're really here just to find me?
Riswynn: We're glad it's now that—
DM: Tell me the mystical place you are from. Everybody is like this? Are you heroes?
Merash: I wouldn't go that far.
Thror: We're all trying our best, right?
Rothfis: I am just a simple tavern owner who can punch and kick with the best of them.
((Brief interjections and postcombat healing or resource bookkeeping))
Rothfis: I think you've got the chance to be a hero, too. We were looking for you because we believe you might be able to help us find someone that we're looking for.
DM: Who are you looking for?

Rothfis: Now, give him the list, the names we've been chatting about, and explain that if he doesn't know them, that any sort of ghosts that have connection to the— I guess the war or the expedition anything that sort of rings the bell with the stories that we've heard about it,
DM: Nora. She is very old, even her spirit is old,
Rothfis: But you've found her, though?
DM: She told me so we were not the only dwarfs. I'm not sure I really believed her until— you must tell me where you're from.
Riswynn: Do names of places other than Bleakhold mean anything to you?
DM: I'm! There— are there places that aren't Bleakhold?
Rothfis: What do you call it?
Thror: What does your home look like? This is a prison that you've been trapped in for decades. This isn't the real world.
DM: Now. No, what is no— Nora, she said. She said it was our— her— our prison destiny, her fate. She said there once were many dwarves.
Rothfis: There still are, and perhaps it's easiest to understand that we come from a place close to where Nora's from.
DM: Nora will never say where she is from.
Rothfis: But you know it's not here.

DM: I suspect my father does not believe. Even Dworic does not believe truly. What else could there be? Look around. Nora she mentions things sometimes. Don't make sense, where food comes from farms, she says.
Rothfis: There are [garbled], and I, I take out the painted soldiers. I say, "This is the most beautiful thing we've seen since we got here, and honestly, it's so sad. It makes me cry."
DM: He grabs them out of his hands.
Rothfis: It's all, uh, it's all just a bit of perspective then. Can you take us to Nora?
DM: You know the way. Tell me a story while we walk.
DM: What is this world you speak of? He begins walking along the cliff to the north.

DM: Come, come! The ghosts won't bother us, spirit ones, anyway. Not on this side of the river. The dwarven ones that— human ghosts can be trouble sometimes, but they never get this far from their camps.
Merash: I think we should follow him.
DM: Who has a story for me?
Riswynn: I mean I'm just, I'm sure it is, what is our life like in, um, the regular world telling the story of cities with carts and horses and inns, and so forth.
DM: Whatever you want, you don't have to literally make up a story if you don't want to,
Riswynn: Because I mean we could tell him the story of retrieving the shield of the Brawnanvils from Raven's Home. That's a long one.
((Brief interjections and postcombat healing or resource bookkeeping))

DM: So as you walk, listening to Riswynn tell the story of a band of adventurers fighting their way through a dwarven ruin, finding fortress of demonic gnolls, killing a demon, rescuing a lost adventurer, are recovering a precious heirloom of the Brawnanvil family. Um! But over the course of an hour, you see like Tak's eyes light up, and he sort of starts to follow Riswynn around. She is definitely a hero. That is what heroes are. I, I didn't, I didn't think they existed.

DM: And as you walk, you see ahead maybe a mile or so, there's a prominence that rises that has a great view back to back to the statue, floating on the top of this prominence, staring at the giant statue, the ghost of an old dwarven woman, and that is where we will stop for tonight.

before: DM: They've all drifted up pretty quickly. I guess the one from the one who just died is still kind of beginning to drift up.
Rothfis: Um! Go ahead. I was going to say I might just float up after it as quick as need be. See if we can chat.

DM: They look—so you float up next to it, you get next to it? This particular ghost seems very faded around the edges. It's like a frayed blanket, or something. Like the features are sort of mostly now, mostly sort of flat, like you can sort of recognize a face, but you wouldn't be able to identify this person if you like saw them again, or if you knew them, like they seemed to be faded somehow.
Rothfis: I say, "Well, we're having ale down below. Would you like to join us?"
DM: Just continues to drift up. Actually go ahead and make up—make a Persuasion check. High DC. You're going to have to find a fresher ghost.
after: DM: Go past midnight. I think it's better to stop there.
